inIlGuard.title: Impermanent Loss Guard (%)
inIlGuard.subtitle: The level of impermanent loss at which the bot skips a rebalance

sections.heading: What it does
sections.body: Before every automatic rebalance, the bot works out what the new position would be worth and compares it against what this NFT was worth on the day it was minted. If the new position would come out more than this percentage below that figure, the rebalance is rejected and the position is left exactly as it is. Nothing is withdrawn, collected, or swapped — the check is a calculation, not a trial run.

sections.heading: Which value it measures against
sections.body: The $usd sum value of the coins of each of the coin types in the position, as taken on the day that the current NFT for the liquidity position was minted. Note that this is not your lifetime deposit into the pool, and not any figure spanning earlier NFTs in the rebalance chain. Each time a rebalance does go through, the new NFT gets its own mint value and the Impermanent Loss Guard (ILG) starts measuring from there.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: The NFT was worth $1,000 at mint and the Impermanent Loss Guard (ILG) is set to 15% (the default). Rebalancing stops if the position would come out below $850. At $910 it rebalances normally; at $820 it is rejected and left alone.

sections.heading: Retries back off, 4 hours to a week
sections.body:
After a rejection the position is left alone rather than re-decided on every poll. The first retry comes 4 hours later, and each further rejection doubles the wait — 4h, 8h, 16h, 32h — up to a ceiling of one week. The moment the Guard lets a rebalance through, the ladder resets to 4 hours.
This bounds how often a rejected rebalance is retried, and the Telegram alert follows the same schedule, so a position blocked for a long stretch reports on a widening interval instead of every poll. The cost is that a position which recovers inside a window waits for it to expire. Rebalance Now is never held by the wait.

sections.heading: A rejection only clears on price
sections.body: This is the part worth knowing. A position rejected by the Impermanent Loss Guard cannot rebalance, so it cannot mint a new NFT, so it cannot get a new mint value to measure against. The bot keeps checking every poll, but nothing it does can lift the block. It lifts when the position’s value recovers above the floor, or when you lower the Guard here. Rebalance Now always works and ignores the Guard entirely.

sections.heading: Choosing a value
sections.body:
The two sides of this trade are not alike, which is why the default is tight. Rebalancing crystallizes the loss: the position is re-minted around today’s price, so a paper loss that a price recovery would have undone becomes permanent. Declining costs you fees — but the check only comes up when a rebalance was due, which usually means the position is already out of range and earning few fees anyway. And fees are what would have to earn that loss back. In a quiet pool that can take longer than you hold the position.
15% (the default) leaves ordinary drawdowns to rebalance and holds back on deep ones.
Higher rebalances through steeper losses, so the position keeps earning — at the price of locking those losses in.
Lower protects harder, and will stop rebalancing often on a swingy pair.
100% effectively turns it off.

sections.heading: What is not included
sections.body: Swap slippage and gas are not part of this figure. A rebalance moves the same dollars from one price range to another, so the projection is the position’s present value — its liquidity plus the pool’s wallet residual, which a rebalance folds back in.

sections.heading: Impermanent gains never block
sections.body: A position worth more than its mint value is above the floor by definition, whatever the Guard is set to, so a gain can never reject a rebalance.

sections.heading: Telegram
sections.body: The Rebalance Rejected Due to Excessive Impermanent Loss alert is on by default — a rejection is otherwise invisible unless you are watching the server log. It carries the figures, says the position was not touched, and links to the User Manual for this explanation rather than repeating it. It follows the retry schedule above, so you get one message per retry, not one per poll.
